item.title: Match Making: Shared Reality Can Enhance Romance
item.description:
Relationships

Match Making: Shared Reality Can Enhance Romance

Many couples experience the seduction of similarity.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Shared reality produces more relationship satisfaction and less life uncertainty.
  • Happy couples balance shared identity and independence.
  • Similarity attracts, but there can be too much of a good thing.
Source: Surprising_Media / Pixabay

Most daters know that relationships come easier when partners can relate to each other. From passion to politics, and everything in between, similar views and values are unifying. Although I have previously written about the value of autonomy within romantic relationships [i], research also corroborates the value of shared, practical experience.

Shared Reality in Romance

Clara D.D. Claveau and Francesca Capozzi (2026) recently explored the concept of shared reality among romantic couples [ii]. They defined shared reality as “the perception of sharing the same interpretation of the world,” which creates meaning within a world which is admittedly complex and uncertain. They conceptualized shared reality in romantic couples within three main areas of research: 1) nonverbal coregulation, 2) verbal communication, and 3) couples’ culture. In their research, Claveau and Capozzi found evidence to support positive outcomes of couples’ shared reality, including a higher degree of relationship satisfaction and less life uncertainty. They also noted, however, less-positive outcomes such as social isolation and identity fusion, which they recognize as clinically important.

Regarding their three main areas of research, Claveau and Capozzi report that their review of the literature indicates that shared reality involves nonverbal patterns of responsiveness, verbal patterns of linguistic similarity, shared references, and culturally similar worldview and values. They note that these shared foundations prompt conditions such as emotion coregulation and cognitive interdependence, contributing to relationship satisfaction. Although Claveau and Capozzi acknowledge that shared reality can create negative outcomes, their research review yields an overall positive association between shared reality and relational satisfaction in couples.

Balancing Identification With Independence

As I have covered in a previous post [iii], having a partner who respects your sense of autonomy is an important part of relational stability and emotional health. In a study appropriately named “Loving Freedom,” [iv] Chin Ming Hui et al. (2013) discussed how close relationships fill important personal needs including the verification and expansion of identity. They found that maintaining a sense of autonomy and self-direction within a relationship enhanced relational well-being when it was supported by a partner.

Ideal relationships likely include a mix of both concepts, allowing partners to identify common ground and celebrate shared values, while also creating and respecting space for expression of individuality. Most people already experience this dynamic in a variety of social contexts from personal to professional, passion to politics. But within the throes of a romantic relationship, finding the balance between shared reality and individuality requires an environment of love, attention, acceptance, patience, and respect. And considering the research, both partners should remain aware of the potential impact shared reality as well as individuality can have on their well-being.

item.title: How Stress and Anxiety Distort Reality
item.description:
Stress

How Stress and Anxiety Distort Reality

Our perceptions are shaped by expectations, stress, anxiety, and expectations.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Even mild stress can distort perception.
  • Anxiety symptoms cause exaggerations and distortions of reality.
  • Daily stress managment practices help us notice more of what is around us.
Source: Photo by Gina Simmons Schneider

While on vacation this summer on the Garden Island of Kauai, my husband and I had booked a botanical gardens tour. The rain made visibility difficult and slowed our driving. Our jeep climbed a muddy dirt road to a secluded parking lot that appeared to have a couple of rustic outbuildings. We were both focused on finding the right place to park and meet for the start of our 2-hour tour.

We saw a rustic open-air hut with greenery on the roof, with many chairs laid out and a podium. We found a place to sit in the indoor/outdoor room and listened as our guide gave the introduction to our tour. After we walked through stunning gardens, sampled chocolates from around the world, and savored fresh cloves, cinnamon, and ambrosia from the cacao fruit, we returned to where we began. I was stunned to notice brightly colored vines streaming in abundance all over the rustic hut. In my hurry to find the right place to go, so as not to miss our tour, I had brushed past the most spectacular flowing vine I had ever seen. Our guide said they were Indian Clock Vines, or Thunbergia Mysorensis. Their bright yellow and red flowers cascaded like wind chimes, covering the entire entrance to the meeting area. Another woman commented, “I didn’t notice them either! Aren’t they gorgeous.” Even though we came to the gardens to view plants, we almost missed seeing the stunning natural beauty hanging right in front of our eyes.

Stress and Attention

Even the mild stress we felt about arriving on time for our tour had distorted our perception of reality. We literally did not see what was right in front of us. Mild stress can increase our processing speed as we attend to a task, such as finding our destination on a map (Shields et al., 2019). The focus of attention on a task shapes what we let fall into the background and what we bring into the foreground. At higher levels, stress can slow our cognitive processing and increase our susceptibility to errors (Khodami et al., 2026).

Selective Attention

The ability to focus our attention on our objectives and not be seduced by distracting stimuli is an important executive brain function (Schneider, 2019). Driving in the rain on dirt roads demanded our focused attention to protect our safety. One reason we did not notice the Indian Clock Vines upon our arrival is that we were focused on finding the right place and making sure we did not miss the tour. We had not yet directed our attention to the plants. Everything but our objective became irrelevant background. Yet, after two hours of exploring, smelling, tasting, and savoring the plants, our vision awoke to the beauty of the place where we began. Our attention is highly shaped by our stress level, anxiety, expectations, and objectives.

article continues after advertisement

Anxiety Can Distort Perception

When we feel anxiety and panic, we can become distracted by physical symptoms of stress such as sweating, dizziness, rapid heart rate, and gastrointestinal disturbances. We often interpret those symptoms as evidence that something is seriously wrong. Exaggerated negative interpretations of these symptoms can increase anxious thoughts that distort reality. Our stress response is real, but the conclusions we draw from those sensations are often not accurate.

Stress and anxiety can also affect memory and decision-making. Research shows that prolonged stress can impair cognitive functions, making it harder to concentrate, recall information, and evaluate situations objectively (Girotti, 2024). Under pressure, people may jump to conclusions, misinterpret events, or overlook important details.

Don’t Believe Everything You See

Selective attention is a necessary executive function of the brain that helps us accomplish our goals. Stress and anxiety can shape our interpretations of reality and lead us to misinterpret or miss important information. This can affect our relationships when we assume others are judging us harshly, rejecting us, or thinking poorly of us. Anxiety can magnify perceived social threats, leading to unnecessary worry and avoidance of social situations.

It helps to accept the fact that our perceptions of reality are limited. You’ve heard the phrase, “Don’t believe everything you think.” I recommend that we don’t believe everything that we see:

  • Our eyes have a limited range and visual field to begin with.
  • Much of what is in front of us we don’t even notice. (Many stay glued to their phones now, even while walking in public.)
  • We can more easily correct our misperceptions when we loosen up the rigid belief in the accuracy of our own perceptions.
article continues after advertisement

Daily stress management practices such as mindfulness, exercise, good sleep, and relaxation in nature can help us notice more and feel happier. You too might even get joyfully gobsmacked by a stunning Indian Clock Vine.

item.title: How Do You Introduce Your Child to Right and Wrong?
item.description:
Parenting

How Do You Introduce Your Child to Right and Wrong?

You can teach kids right and wrong whether or not you have a religious affiliation.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Parents can model loving, caring, compassionate behavior starting early in a child's life.
  • At age three, parents can begin to talk about The Golden Rule.
  • Parents can discuss how to treat others and how to make good choices in behavior.
  • Parents can ask children to consider how their actions make others feel.

Often parents think about how to get their children to understand right from wrong. Maybe a better way to think about it is to consider how to handle the development of a sense of ethics and morality in your children. Do you have any idea where to start? Or, in all the hustle bustle of daily life, has this part of your child's education gone by the wayside?

These days, only 30% of people in the US attend religious services regularly and only 37% hold a membership at a house of worship. And yet church, synagogue, and mosque were traditionally the places children learned about ethical behavior and morality.

What are parents to do?

First, parents should know that the origins of empathy, compassion, and respect come from a child's first relationships. If parents model these qualities in the early years of a child's life and insist that their young children treat them with honesty, humility, and love, children will have a strong beginning foundation in ethical behavior.

Second, parents can talk to their children starting as early as age two or three about the right way is to treat others.

Third, as early as age three, parents can begin to talk about The Golden Rule.

The basic idea that we should treat others as we would like to be treated is something that even the youngest children can begin to think about. And while some people may think that The Golden Rule evolved from one religious tradition, such as Christianity, this is not true. Treating others as we would like to be treated is a universal ethical principle found in most faiths.

Many years before the birth of Jesus, Confucius said, "Do not do unto others what you don't want done to yourself." The Prophet Mohammed said, "None of you truly believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself" and the Jewish sage, Hillel, said, "That which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow." Later, in the teachings of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew (7:12), we read, "Do to others whatever you would like them to do to you."

Fourth, and finally, as children get older, parents can talk with them about making choices in how they behave and how they treat others. Parents can ask a child to begin to use what is called mentalization by asking, "How do you think what you did made the other person feel?"

Parents can model this kind of self-reflection by talking about things they have done that they later regretted. They can talk about their own thought process at the time and afterward and how they came to see that their own behavior was not the best choice.

article continues after advertisement

Beginning your child's ethical education sounds complicated, but it doesn't have to be. Helping children to evaluate their own actions and providing them with a basic compass for judging whether what they have done was the best choice is something all parents can do, with or without a religious orientation.

item.title: Why We Need Neurodiversity Pride
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Why We Need Neurodiversity Pride

Personal Perspective: Neurodiversity pride is neurodiversity survival.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • June 11-17 is Neurodiversity Pride Week.
  • Neurodiversity is a natural kind of human diversity, but it is stigmatized.
  • Our society needs to expand what it means to be acceptably human.
Source: Intervex / Wikimedia Commons

June 11-17 is Neurodiversity Pride Week. Why, you might wonder, is such a pride week important?

This month, I turn 50 years old. With the help of hindsight, I can see that the story of my life is one of neurodiversity. Diagnosed with ADHD in the first grade—a near impossibility for a girl in the early 1980s—then diagnosed with bipolar disorder when I was in college, exactly when people show symptoms. Diagnosed with autism in my early 40s, part of the “lost generation“ of autistic adults.

The story of my life is also one of hiding my neurodiversity. In middle school and high school, I hid because I was embarrassed to be myself. The times when my true self slipped through, I was socially punished. Even then, I knew I wasn’t quite right, never fully a part of the social group that was ostensibly mine, a freak, a weirdo. I tried so hard for social acceptance, but it never came. And that trying came at the cost of loving and accepting myself. None of my so-called friends from high school speak to me anymore. Instead, I’ve gradually reconnected with the other freaks and weirdos.

Later, throughout my education and career as a professor, I hid my neurodiversity because I was afraid of getting kicked out of school or fired from my job. Nobody wants to be stuck in a room with a person with bipolar disorder; we are scary people. Unpredictable. Violent. At minimum, we are erratic and unreliable.

This “hiding” that I am describing has other names: masking, performing neurotypicality, or social camouflaging. Many, if not most, neurodivergent people mask. It is a survival skill.

But masking comes with a steep cost. It is exhausting and leads to burnout, anxiety, depression, and suicide. Autistic people are 60% more likely to die by suicide than the general population. Masking to fit in with the neurotypical world is, in the end, not a survival skill at all. It can kill us.

I am not “differently abled”; my impairments are real. I struggle with insomnia and anxiety. With meltdowns and shutdowns and depression.

But impairments are different than disability. The second is a social problem, not a personal one. I am disabled by a society that makes it difficult and sometimes impossible to be myself. To be autistic or otherwise neurodivergent is to be part of a stigmatized social group, a social outcast.

Although neurodiversity is a natural kind of human diversity, such as height or hair color, unlike those traits, ours are stigmatized, criticized, unwanted, and rejected. Kids are kicked off of sports teams, bullied by fellow classmates, and unsupported in school. Adults are criticized at work for being rude (because we might struggle with small talk), or difficult (because we might need accommodations).

article continues after advertisement

Neurodiversity pride is about survival—for me, as I head into my second half century, and for my children as they make their way through their teenage years. Neurodiversity advocates like me speak out about our neurodivergences because other people cannot. They will lose their jobs. They might be in prison, where too many neurodivergent people end up, or lost to us forever.

Despite my impairments, I have never expected the world to bend for me. I have always bent myself into the shape that the world found acceptable. But that is not the life I want for my children, your children, or anyone coming behind me.

I want to broaden what it means to be acceptably human. And yes, to take this kind of stand requires pride, the arrogant and unwavering belief that I’m doing the right thing. Neurodiversity pride.

Changing the world is a task that is never finished. Instead, it is a process, a journey. My allies, my friends, my loved ones: Join me on this journey.

item.title: You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!
item.description:
Parenting

You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!

Why parents of struggling adult children get hung up on helping vs. enabling.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Not all struggling adult children are struggling in obvious ways.
  • Many conscientious parents become trapped in cycles of guilt and rescuing.
  • The most powerful shift parents can make is moving from fixer to coach.

We hear a lot these days about struggling adult children and the heartbreak parents experience when communication is cut off. Yet far less attention is paid to a reality I see almost every day in my parent coaching practice: Parents who remain deeply involved in their adult children's lives but feel trapped by ongoing crisis, dependence, and demands for help.

In my forthcoming book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me!, I explore a huge dilemma that countless parents face today. Their adult child may be struggling with resentment, depression, anxiety, employment, finances, motivation, or independence. In these cases, their child has not "just walked away" but has not yet stepped into adulthood.

The Staunchly Embedded Belief of Being Wronged by Their Parents

One of the biggest misconceptions about struggling adult children is that they all fit the same profile. That is not the case. Some may struggle with anxiety, depression, ADHD, addiction, or chronic overthinking and indecision. Yet I have worked with parents of struggling adult children who hold impressive jobs, such as doctors, architects, engineers, or project managers—who appear successful to the outside world. What they tend to share is a lingering conviction that they have been wronged and that their parents bear responsibility for the emotional struggles they face.

The parents I work with are in pain because they are in a truly impossible bind. Most admit they were not perfect and made mistakes. Most are also reflective and value working through conflicts and healing their relationships with their adult children.

At the same time, they worry that helping too much will enable dependence—and they worry that helping too little will feel like abandonment. Meanwhile, they often receive a message that may be spoken directly, hinted at, or said through the language of fluent sarcasm. It often goes something like: "My life is not where it should be, and somehow it is your fault."

What Exhausts Parents Is Feeling Their Help Is Not Enough

One parent who sought me out for coaching was "stuck paying out reparations for messing up" their adult child's life. They sadly struggled with self-blame until they were able to realize that no amount of money was going to buy the love and understanding from their bitter adult child. It turns out the adult child wanted something money could not buy: calm, constructive, empathetic conversations to heal. Of course, the adult child first had to work through their anger-related thoughts and feelings, to finally talk things through more constructively.

One father told me, "I feel guilty when I don't help, and I feel guilty when I do." This statement captures the emotional dilemma so many parents face. A mother I have been coaching has learned to navigate the longstanding pattern of her daughter's demands to "prove her love." Financial assistance, help finding jobs (and then the command to back off from supportively asking about jobs), and advice about relationships in response to crisis calls were demanded and expected—but not appreciated.

article continues after advertisement

The Shift From Fixer to Coach

One of the most important shifts parents can make is from fixer to coach. Fixers rush in to solve problems, prevent mistakes, smooth over consequences, and prevent discomfort. Coaches listen, empathize, and encourage, but they resist taking ownership of problems that belong to their adult child.

This shift is not easy; I have worked with many parents to navigate their natural resistances (mostly due to unhealthy guilt) to get there. Many parents fear that stepping back is abandoning their child. In reality, adopting a coaching mindset conveys a powerful message: "I believe you are capable of handling more than you think." The goal is not to stop caring; it's to stop carrying.

item.title: 15 Signs Your Church Functions Like a Cult
item.description:
Religion

15 Signs Your Church Functions Like a Cult

Religious cults mandate strict separatism, censorship, and autocratic control.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • Uncritical defensiveness of religion without regard for human welfare can lead to religious fundamentalism.
  • Fundamentalist religious abuse can involve anti-intellectualism, authoritarianism, castes, and ritual shaming.
  • Cult abuse and fundamentalist abuse overlap in terms of separatism, censorship, and autocratic leadership.
Source: Karl Fredrickson / Unsplash

Most people presume that religious institutions are safe spaces and that religious leaders rarely distort or weaponize doctrine for harm. This general sentiment persists, even among people who are familiar with religious corruption and the many wars, holocausts, hate groups, colonial empires, and caste systems that religious leaders have influenced throughout history.

Religious psychologists attribute this denial to the fact that many people turn to religion to find emotional catharsis, to escape grief or tragedy, or to find a sense of control or certainty about the unknown.

Critical thinking can be less important to people whose religiosity is emotionally driven. For these people, religion is often connected to their will to live and is the primary lens through which they make meaning of life. Consequently, a bias emerges that defies critical thinking: They misperceive any critique of religious harm within a particular context as an attack on religion altogether. They are unable to see how one can critique a thing precisely because they see immense value in it and therefore wish to do right by it.

Emotional bias to this degree lends itself to religious fundamentalism, or a movement to interpret religious scriptures or dogmas strictly and literally while also pursuing revival of a romanticized/mythical past and juxtaposing the alleged purity of one’s in-group against the alleged impurity of “worldly” out-groups.

Source: Jakub Pierozynski / Unsplash

Religious fundamentalists/zealots typically have an absolutist, defensive, and militant view of religion. That their entire life is religion means their defense of religion rarely has reasonable limits, like exceptions for sexual abuse, fraudulence, or bigotry. Instead, they’re defensive of religion even when what or whom they’re defending directly contradicts their religion’s most basic ethical tenets (e.g., the Ten Commandments). They need to believe religion is perfect to feel powerful.

Such fundamentalists/zealots are often bystanders or proponents of religious abuse. While anti-intellectualism is a primary vehicle of religious abuse, abusive dogma is also reinforced by authoritarianism, castes, public humiliation rituals, and an organizational culture of spiritual one-upmanship/posturing/virtue signaling.

article continues after advertisement

Fundamentalists/zealots justify these harmful practices by claiming that they have the right to their own identity. Yet, constructive identity does not need to emerge at the expense of any other person or group. It’s not a zero-sum game.

And this is where things get cultish.

An "us-vs.-the-world" mentality is one of the most significant points of overlap between religious abuse and cult abuse. In both instances, abuse often sounds like accusations of betrayal after requests for accountability from leadership or invitations to consider critical thinking that allegedly questions a leader’s anointing. Any criticism or feedback—no matter how constructive—threatens the group’s illusion of superiority, and that voice must be censored or ousted. At this point, many survivors of religious or cult abuse awaken to their indoctrination.

Research on the "us vs. the world" mentality of religious cults also refers to this as "dispensing of existence," which describes how fundamentalist groups and cults arrogate to themselves the authority or privilege of deciding who is spiritually or psychologically valid. This in-group bias is reinforced by:

  • accountability deflection via a persecution complex: weaponizing the "us-vs.-the-world" framework to detract credibility from whistleblower evidence/testimonies of abuse

  • isolation as a control mechanism: warning members that non-approved professionals or relatives will corrupt them

  • milieu control: limiting information exchange/flow within an environment—i.e., thought/mind control

Source: Nathan Mullet / Unsplash

Integrating my previous research on religious abuse with insights on the organizational, leadership, and doctrinal dynamics of cults results in an original framework for understanding the signs of cultish religious abuse.

Extrapolating this framework to religious sects other than Christian fundamentalists may be possible; however, the framework is based on the specific context of fundamentalist churches, since my clinical work in this realm has focused on that particular population. The framework is not a generalization about all churches writ large.

The Signs of Cultish Religious Abuse

Dogma

  1. Literalism: Approaching ethical dilemmas with black-and-white thinking, even when that mindset is harmful, high-risk, impractical, or inhumane.
  2. Fatalism: Celebrating natural disasters, pandemics, wars, etc., as miraculous signs that the rapture is near, without any concern for those negatively impacted.
  3. Theocracy: Believing that God’s alleged appointment of all leaders shields them from impeachment or democratic accountability, even if they’re bigoted, exploitative, or inhumane.
  4. Anti-modernity: Weaponizing "the good old days"—or an oversimplified version of history—to dismiss valid critiques from younger people and frame generational “rebellion” as the problem.
  5. Anti-humanism: Believing that you are pleasing God by denying help or human rights to people who do not share your specific denominational beliefs.
article continues after advertisement

Social Punishment

  1. Groupthink: Calling anyone who fact-checks or questions the leader a demon, a false prophet, the Antichrist, the Enemy, a Jezebel, or an orphan spirit, or worldly, secular, earthly, carnal, etc.
  2. Humiliation: Punishing those who dissent or give feedback by saying they're publicly slandering you, publicly sharing what you’ve disclosed in private, or publicly casting doubt on your private relationship with God.
  3. Uniformity: Accusing anyone who encourages critical thinking or cultural pluralism of having an “agenda,” a plot, or an ulterior motive to tempt people away from God.
  4. Favoritism: Accusing people of being jealous when they call out hypocrisy in a way that excuses leaders/the in-crowd from the same backlash and scrutiny as “regular” followers.
  5. Victim-blaming/playing: Blaming conflict on a person's unwillingness to tolerate bullying, while never confronting leaders and letting abusive leaders pretend that self-defense against abuse is a “spiritual attack” on them.

Self-Perception

  1. Suppression: Being discouraged from trusting your nervous system when your intuition or gut instinct signals that you’re unsafe or being targeted.
  2. Narcissistic victimhood: Believing the ancient persecution of your group is recurring in response to valid critiques when your group’s defensiveness actually mirrors ancient oppressors.
  3. Group superiority: Being indoctrinated into an “us-vs.-the-world” worldview that condemns coexistence and casts strangers as deceptive and calculating rivals in a “spiritual warfare.”
  4. Co-dependency: Believing that changing your circumstances without approval/direction from leadership is going against God’s will, instead of realizing your leaders are playing God.
  5. Self-deprecation: Encouraging negative self-talk about innate brokenness/depravity, yet conflating dignity/self-worth with boasting, showing off, and not giving God the glory.

Recovery From Cult Abuse and Religious Trauma

Source: John Price / Unsplash

Survivors of cultish religious abuse often suffer from a specific form of post-traumatic stress syndrome known as religious trauma syndrome. While defining and unpacking the symptomatology is beyond the scope of this post, you can read more about the disorder in my previous posts. What is important to remember is that religious trauma is not simply about the struggle to unlearn harmful dogma and fill a void. It also involves immense grief in the aftermath of losing an entire community and social support system—not to mention grappling with identity erasure, systemic gaslighting, and severe fear of venturing into a world that has been stigmatized as wholly dangerous. If you or someone you know is a survivor of cult abuse or religious trauma syndrome, reach out to a mental health professional who specializes in this particular sub-area of trauma recovery.

article continues after advertisement

item.title: New Research Shows Optimism May Reduce the Risk of Dementia
item.description:
Optimism

New Research Shows Optimism May Reduce the Risk of Dementia

How to strengthen your optimism and increase your ability to flourish.

Posted June 17, 2026

Key points
  • New research reveals the health benefits of optimism.
  • Research shows optimism may reduce the risk of dementia.
  • Optimists are healthier, less likely to be depressed, and better able to respond to life's challenges.
  • The good news is that optimism can be increased with 3 simple interventions.

New research highlights the health benefits of optimism. A recent longitudinal study of over 9000 older adults associated higher optimism with better cognitive function and reduced risk of dementia (Stenlund et al., 2026).

Source: Tobias Nordhausen (2012). Happy People. Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons attribution

Optimists are “people who expect good things to happen to them,” feeling positive about the future (Carver et al., 2010). Being optimistic can help us thrive in many ways. Research has associated optimism with better emotional and physical health, lower likelihood of depression, better immune function, greater academic success, the ability to persevere amidst life’s challenges, and the capacity to learn and grow even after trauma (Carver et al., 2010; Rasmussen et al., 2009).

The good news for us is that research has revealed that we can increase our optimism with psychological interventions or practices (Malouff & Schutte, 2017). Whatever your level of optimism, you can boost it with one of these practices:

1. Best Possible Self Intervention

Clearly imagine a future in which you have achieved your goals and everything has turned out as well as possible (Loveday et al., 2018). To connect with your best possible self, take time to reflect. Imagine your future, visualize what you’d like to achieve, and imagine what it would look like and feel like if you realized all your deepest dreams. Now write down what you’ve imagined in as much detail as possible (King, 2001).

2. Self-Compassion Intervention

When dealing with difficult feelings, try these three steps to build your self-compassion and strengthen your optimism:

  • Mindfulness. Instead of attacking or shaming yourself, tune in to how you feel. Ask “What am I feeling?” and name your feelings, whatever they might be. For example, “I feel sad. . . scared. . . anxious. . .ashamed. . .hurt. . . angry. . . worried. . .” or something else.
  • Common humanity. Remind yourself that it’s only human to feel this way. Tell yourself, “It’s OK. No one’s perfect.”
  • Kindness to yourself. Actively soothe yourself with kind words, saying something like, “I know this is hard and you’re really hurting right now. I’m here for you” (Neff, 2011, pp. 103-104).
article continues after advertisement

3. Gratitude Intervention

Pause to acknowledge and be thankful for the good things in your life each day (Emmons, 2007; Puente-Dias & Cavazos-Arroyo, 2022). Here are three ways to cultivate greater gratitude:

  • Begin the day with gratitude. When you wake up in the morning, think of one thing to look forward to. This can be anything from appreciating the taste of your morning coffee to beginning a new project, meeting with a friend, enjoying your favorite hobby, or something else.
  • Pause for moments of gratitude. During the day, pause periodically to focus on something you’re grateful for. For example, you can appreciate the beauty of sunlight shining through the trees, the bright blue sky overhead, a greeting from a neighbor, a message from a friend, smiling at a loved one, and more.
  • Practice gratitude at the end of the day. Research has found that listing three things you’re grateful for at the end of the day can relieve stress, improve your health, help you overcome adversity, and build greater hope (Emmons & McCullough, 2003; Emmons, 2007). Try this practice yourself by keeping a gratitude journal, writing down three things you’re grateful for at the end of each day.

Now it’s your turn. How will you strengthen your optimism and increase your ability to thrive?
